Ladies and gentlemen, the tragic death of Corporal Pat Tillman is a profound loss for his family, for our nation, and for all who value the selfless service of our military personnel. I understand the depth of their grief and the need for answers. Pat Tillman embodied the spirit of sacrifice and dedication to our country, and it is our solemn duty to ensure that his memory is honored with the truth.

The Defense Department shares the Tillman family's desire to uncover the facts surrounding his death. We are committed to conducting a thorough and transparent investigation, one that will bring clarity and closure. The repeated statements of 'I don't recall' from former officials underscore the need for a comprehensive review that will not only address the circumstances of Corporal Tillman's death but also ensure accountability and transparency.

To the Tillman family, I pledge that we will pursue the truth with relentless determination. We owe it to Pat, we owe it to the brave men and women who serve, and we owe it to the American people. This administration is dedicated to uncovering the facts and ensuring that justice is served. We will not rest until we have the full story, and we will communicate openly with the Tillman family every step of the way.

This commitment is not just a promise; it is a solemn vow to honor the memory of Corporal Tillman and to uphold the integrity of our military and our government. We will conduct this investigation with the seriousness it deserves and will ensure that the findings are made public, so that Pat Tillman's legacy is remembered with the truth.

Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your questions. On the matter of the Iranian nuclear issue, I want to emphasize that progress has been made. The United States and Russia have come to a consensus that Iran should not possess a nuclear weapon. This is a significant development. It's imperative that the Iranian government understands that our united stance is unwavering—they should not have a weapon. This clarity in our message is crucial; it will bring us closer to persuading Iran to choose a path that does not involve nuclear armament.

We have made a clear choice to work together towards a common goal. This is considerable progress. The ball is now in Iran's court. We have offered a deal: if Iran verifiably suspends its enrichment program, we will engage in negotiations, sitting side by side. This is a fair and reasonable proposition.

Currently, we are negotiating together to send a unified message to Iran. Our intention is to come to the negotiating table, but it is ultimately Iran's decision to make. The Iranian people deserve a better future than one isolated by their government's actions. 

We have seen some press collusion, an old tactic, but one that doesn't change our commitment to transparency and progress. Moving forward, we anticipate continued dialogue and diplomacy. Our hope is that Iran will recognize the benefits of cooperation over confrontation and choose a path that leads to peace and prosperity for all. Thank you.

Thank you for the question. Let me first address the matter of striking inside Pakistan. The sovereignty of Pakistan is a cornerstone of our relationship. We have a mutual interest in combating terrorism, and we've made it clear that any action against Usama bin Laden or Al Qaida is not a matter of permission—it's our right and our duty to protect our citizens. We are in constant communication with Pakistan about these matters, ensuring that any operation is coordinated to the extent possible, given the circumstances. We are not seeking to infringe upon Pakistan's sovereignty, but we are committed to taking the necessary actions to secure justice for the victims of 9/11 and to protect our national security.

As for the tribal deal, I am fully satisfied with the assurances provided. The President has made it unequivocally clear that this deal is not about legitimizing the Taliban or allowing Al Qaida to operate freely. It's about stabilizing the region to prevent the Talibanization of the people and to ensure that the Afghan government can take root and provide security for its citizens. The President's commitment to rejecting the Taliban and Al Qaida is unwavering, and I trust his judgment and his vision for a secure and peaceful future in the region. We are on the same page, and our strategies are aligned to achieve these goals.

Thank you for the question. It's been a year of significant progress and ongoing challenges since Katrina. We've made substantial commitments to aid the recovery efforts in New Orleans and the surrounding areas. Our government has allocated over $110 billion to this cause, a testament to our dedication to helping the people affected by this devastating storm.

A considerable portion of these funds has been directed towards immediate needs such as housing assistance for those displaced, infrastructure repair, and the removal of storm debris. Mississippi has been quite effective in clearing their dry debris, achieving an impressive 97 to 98 percent removal rate. In contrast, Louisiana has been slower in this process, and we're working closely with their officials to expedite the removal of waterlogged debris.

The recovery is a marathon, not a sprint. While we've made substantial progress, there's still much to be done. Ensuring that the funds are used efficiently and effectively is crucial. We're also focusing on long-term recovery efforts, including sustainable rebuilding and strengthening the levees to protect against future storms.

To the people of New Orleans, I want to reiterate our commitment to your recovery. It's going to take time, but we're in this for the long haul. We're working tirelessly to ensure that your city not only recovers but thrives once again. Together, we will overcome these challenges and build a stronger, more resilient Gulf Coast.

No, I don't regret the decision to remove Saddam Hussein from power. I believe it made the world a safer place. It's important to remember that in my line of work, we don't get the luxury of second chances. However, looking back, I acknowledge that I could have used more effective rhetoric to communicate two key points: one, that we genuinely attempted to exhaust all diplomatic avenues in Iraq; and two, that I personally abhor war. 

I understand the concerns and the differing viewpoints on this matter, and I've heard them all. Journalists like Steven Lee Myers and Dan Eggen have reported extensively on this issue, and their work is invaluable in keeping the public informed. What's crucial is that the decision to act was made after careful consideration and with the belief that it was necessary to protect our national and global security. 

In hindsight, I could have articulated these points more clearly, but the decision to confront the threat posed by Saddam Hussein was the right one. It's a decision I stand by, even as we continue to work towards a stable and peaceful Iraq.

As the President of the United States, I understand that diplomacy is a complex and often time-consuming process. The situation with Iran is no exception. We are committed to resolving this issue through dialogue and cooperation with a broad coalition of nations. The recent resolution, which brought together a diverse group of countries including China, Russia, the EU-3, and the United States, sends a unified and powerful message to Iran.

While I recognize that this process could indeed take some time, I am hopeful that our collective efforts will yield positive results. The strength of this international coalition is a testament to our shared commitment to addressing the challenges posed by Iran's nuclear program through diplomatic means.

We are prepared to engage in sustained negotiations and will continue to work tirelessly to find a peaceful resolution. It is my belief that by maintaining this united front and demonstrating patience, we increase the likelihood of achieving a lasting and beneficial outcome for all parties involved. We are committed to this path and remain hopeful for a resolution that ensures Iran's nuclear program is peaceful and that the region, and indeed the world, can live in security and peace.

Thank you for the question. The integrity and dedication of U.S. Attorney Patrick Fitzgerald to the pursuit of justice have been nothing short of exemplary. His work in addressing corruption has not only been crucial to the rule of law but has also served to reinforce the public's trust in our legal system. As President, I am deeply committed to maintaining the highest standards of integrity within the Department of Justice.

Regarding Mr. Fitzgerald's current status, it's accurate to say that he serves at the pleasure of the President. However, my administration values the expertise and commitment he has shown throughout his tenure. We are actively considering the best way to ensure that his valuable contributions continue to benefit our nation's justice system.

While I cannot commit to a specific decision at this moment, it is important to note that we are looking at various options that would allow Mr. Fitzgerald to continue his impactful work. This could include a formal reappointment or exploring other roles within the Department of Justice where his skills and experience can be equally effective. We are committed to making a decision that respects his service and recognizes the importance of his ongoing efforts to combat corruption.

In any case, the decision will be made with the utmost consideration for the public interest and the continued pursuit of justice. Thank you for bringing this important matter to our discussion.

Mr. President, the question of corporate taxes is indeed a complex one that touches on our nation's economic competitiveness. As we've discussed, the idea being floated within the Treasury Department circles is to examine whether our current corporate tax rates are creating a disadvantage for American businesses in the global marketplace. The premise here is straightforward: if our tax structure makes it more difficult for businesses to compete internationally, then it indirectly impacts job creation here at home.

I've made it clear that any proposal to alter our tax code would need to be revenue-neutral, meaning it wouldn't increase the deficit. Instead, the focus would be on simplification—streamlining the Tax Code to eliminate complexities and loopholes. This could potentially allow for a reduction in rates while still maintaining the same level of tax revenue. The goal is to make our tax system more efficient and fair, which could encourage businesses to invest domestically and grow.

I understand that this is a sensitive issue. Many powerful interests have a stake in the current tax code, and changing it won't be easy. As I told a group of writers yesterday, it's much easier to add a tax preference than to remove one. However, I believe it's crucial for us to continually assess our competitive standing in the global economy. Treasury Secretary Hank Paulson has highlighted the sentiment among many that our Tax Code is a hindrance rather than a help in this regard.

In conclusion, while no final decisions have been made, the conversation is about ensuring that our tax policies support a strong, competitive economy that benefits all Americans. It's a dialogue that requires careful consideration and bipartisan cooperation.

Steve, let me be clear: the United States does not engage in torture, nor do we condone it. Our nation's values are deeply rooted in the dignity and worth of every human being. The program I've outlined is designed to question enemy combatants in a manner that is consistent with our laws and our values. We must find a balance between obtaining critical information necessary for our national security and adhering to the principles of justice and human rights.

The Detainee Treatment Act, which Senator McCain and I worked on together, sets the standard for how we treat detainees. It prohibits cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. Our proposal seeks to provide clarity and legal definition to the standards set forth in Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, ensuring that our professionals can carry out their duties without fear of prosecution under ambiguous international law.

The concern about secret hearings and coerced evidence is a valid one. Transparency and due process are essential in our legal system. That's why our approach includes clear guidelines and oversight. We must ensure that any information obtained is reliable and obtained through lawful means.

As for the argument that our proposal puts U.S. troops at risk, I understand the concern. Our military men and women deserve the best protection possible. However, the current ambiguity in the law could potentially put them at risk as well. By clarifying the standards under which we operate, we can better protect our troops and ensure they act within a legal framework that is both just and effective.

We must remember that the Geneva Conventions themselves were designed to protect those who fall under their jurisdiction. By adhering to their principles while providing our forces with the clarity they need, we can uphold our values and protect our national security. This debate is about ensuring that we are both strong in defense and true to our ideals. It's a responsibility I take very seriously.

Good morning. The situation in Iraq is indeed grave and complex, and it's natural for people to look for clear-cut answers in the midst of such turmoil. However, it's important to base our understanding on the most current and comprehensive information available. After speaking with our Ambassador and General Casey this morning, as well as consulting with Iraqi officials, it's clear that while there is no shortage of violence and challenges, the picture is not as simple as a civil war.

The consensus among our experts is that while there is undoubtedly a significant amount of violence, Al-Qaeda continues to sow discord, Saddam loyalists are still a threat, and reprisals are taking place, the Baghdad security plan is showing signs of progress. The key indicators for me are whether the unity government is making strides in governance, whether they are addressing critical issues like oil and federalism through political means, and if there's a genuine effort towards reconciliation.

Our military leaders in Anbar Province, in particular, have made it clear that while Al-Qaeda is indeed a formidable presence and the region remains dangerous, the narrative of Al Anbar's loss to Al-Qaeda is not accurate. They are confident that the security plan is having an impact and that Iraqi forces are increasingly capable.

So, to answer your question directly, while the situation is dire and the violence is unacceptable, the conditions on the ground do not yet meet the threshold of a civil war. The focus must remain on supporting the Iraqi government and its efforts to stabilize the country and move towards a peaceful future.

Ladies and gentlemen, the decision regarding the involvement of U.S. troops in international missions, such as the proposed peacekeeping force in Lebanon, is not taken lightly. It's rooted in a careful consideration of our nation's capabilities, the strategic interests of the United States, and the potential impact on global perceptions.

Historically, Lebanon has been a complex region, and the presence of U.S. troops has been a sensitive matter. We've learned from past experiences and are mindful of the need to approach such commitments with caution. Our military is currently engaged in multiple operations around the world, and it's essential to ensure that our forces are not overextended.

Moreover, the perception of U.S. involvement in certain regions can sometimes complicate rather than facilitate peace efforts. This is particularly true in areas where the U.S. is seen as having contentious or controversial motives. In the case of Darfur, for instance, while the humanitarian crisis is grave, the deployment of U.S. troops could potentially overshadow the peacekeeping mission with political and military complications.

Instead, we are offering logistical and command and control support to the international force in Lebanon. This approach allows us to contribute effectively to the mission without the political and military challenges that might arise from a direct U.S. military presence. By providing these critical support elements, we can help ensure the success and stability of the peacekeeping operation, thereby supporting our broader goals of regional peace and security.

I understand the concern and the need for clarity on this matter. Let me elaborate further on our current stance and capabilities regarding ballistic missile defense.

Three days after North Korea's missile launch, we are still in the process of analyzing the trajectory data. The complexity of these missiles and the vast distances involved make precise tracking and prediction challenging. However, I want to assure you that our intelligence community is working diligently to ascertain the full extent of the missile's path.

As for our national ballistic missile system, it is indeed in its nascent stages. Our current systems are modest, as I mentioned, and are part of an ongoing research and development effort to enhance our defensive capabilities. These systems are designed to intercept and neutralize incoming missiles under various scenarios, including those that might be aimed at the United States.

While I cannot provide a specific probability of success for these systems—given that they are still being tested and refined—I can tell you that our commitment to a robust and effective missile defense is unwavering. The threat posed by a nontransparent regime like North Korea, which appears willing to launch missiles without declaring their intent or contents, underscores the critical importance of developing and perfecting these systems.

In the hypothetical scenario where a missile was indeed headed towards the United States, our goal would be to engage it with our missile defense systems as early as possible, using a layered approach to increase the chances of interception. This involves a combination of land-based, sea-based, and potentially air-based interceptors, working in concert to neutralize the threat.

It's important to note that while we continue to build and test these systems, we also engage in diplomatic efforts to reduce the threat of missile proliferation and to promote transparency and dialogue with nations like North Korea. Our ultimate aim is to ensure the safety and security of the American people and our allies.

The question of the United Nations resolutions and the Israeli settlements is indeed a critical one. As President, my administration's stance is clear: we believe that the settlement activity is an obstacle to peace and a hindrance to the negotiations process. The United Nations resolutions that call for an end to the occupation and the establishment of a Palestinian state are not merely suggestions; they are internationally recognized principles that we support.

We have consistently urged Israel to engage in negotiations in good faith with the elected leadership of the Palestinian Territory. This is not just about adhering to past resolutions; it's about creating a viable path forward that can lead to a permanent solution. The status quo is unsustainable, and it's time to break free from the cycle of violence and conflict.

The opportunity before us is to redefine the future for both Palestinians and Israelis. By negotiating a state that is democratic and viable, we offer a hopeful alternative to the current situation. This is not just about ending the occupation; it's about building a lasting peace that benefits all parties involved.

The choice for the Palestinian people should be clear: do they want a future based on a democratic state living side by side with Israel, or do they wish to continue under the status quo? We are confident that, given this choice, the Palestinian people will opt for peace and a brighter future.

Our commitment to this process is unwavering, and we have communicated this to Prime Minister Olmert and President Bush. The statements from Secretary of State Rice reflect our shared understanding of the importance of addressing the settlements issue. Together, we are working towards a solution that respects the rights and aspirations of both the Palestinian and Israeli people.

The attack on the Beirut airport is indeed a matter of grave concern. It underscores the volatile nature of the situation in Lebanon and the broader Middle East. As President, my foremost priority is to ensure that actions taken by any party do not undermine the Siniora Government. This is critical because a stable, democratic Lebanon is essential for peace in the region. We've worked tirelessly, alongside the international community, to see Syria's influence in Lebanon reduced, culminating in U.N. Resolutions 1559 and 1680.

It's important to remember that Lebanon's path to democracy is fragile and must be supported. Any action that threatens this government could have disastrous consequences, potentially leading to the very instability we seek to avoid. We've made our stance clear: we support the Siniora Government and oppose any efforts to topple it.

At the same time, we recognize the right of any nation to defend itself against terrorism. The terrorists targeting Lebanon are not just attacking a country; they're attacking the very idea of peace. They seek to disrupt the progress toward a two-state solution, two democracies living side by side in peace—a vision that is clear, achievable, and essential for the region's future.

The attack on the Beirut airport raises the specter of a wider conflict. It is a stark reminder of the challenges we face. Our goal must remain focused on supporting Lebanon's sovereignty and democratic institutions while combating the terrorists who seek to derail peace. The roadmap offers a path forward, but it requires the commitment of all parties to work together. The last thing we need is a wider war. Our efforts must be directed towards preventing that outcome and ensuring that Lebanon's democratic aspirations are not thwarted by violence. Thank you.

They seek to disrupt the progress toward a two-state solution, two democracies living side by side in peace—a vision that is clear, achievable, and essential for the region's future.

The attack on the Beirut airport raises the specter of a wider conflict. It is a stark reminder of the challenges we face. Our goal must remain focused on supporting Lebanon's sovereignty and democratic institutions while combating the terrorists who seek to derail peace. The roadmap offers a path forward, but it requires the commitment of all parties to work together. The last thing we need is a wider war. Our efforts must be directed towards preventing that outcome and ensuring that Lebanon's democratic aspirations are not thwarted by violence. Thank you.

Ladies and gentlemen, the fight against terrorism is a complex and multifaceted endeavor, one that we have been engaged in for quite some time now. As we forge ahead, we inevitably encounter challenges—these are the hurdles that come with such a monumental task. But let me assure you, we are not only meeting these challenges head-on but also overcoming them. Our resolve is unwavering, and we continue to advance to the next phase of this critical mission.

Four years ago, we launched a concerted effort to dislodge the terrorists from Afghanistan, to ensure they could no longer govern that nation. This was followed by extensive operations to apprehend or expel them from the region. Once this was achieved, we turned our attention to rebuilding the country—building roads, schools, health clinics, and ensuring access to education and basic services for all its citizens. We are now at a pivotal stage, striving to establish a lasting stability and to finally eradicate the terrorist presence from Afghanistan.

While our desire is to achieve this sooner rather than later, we must acknowledge that patience is required. The process will take time, and we must remain steadfast in our commitment to see it through to the end.

On the issue of narcotics, it is indeed a significant problem, not just for Afghanistan but for the region and the world. It is an embarrassment to our nation, a stark reminder of the years of desperation and hopelessness that have gripped our people. Many families, facing uncertainty and the loss of their livelihoods, have turned to poppy cultivation as a means of survival. We have made strides in combating this issue, with some areas showing positive results, while others continue to pose challenges. This is a problem that Afghanistan must address with the support of our friends and allies, including the United States. It is a shared responsibility, and we are committed to working tirelessly towards a solution.

Ladies and gentlemen, I want to address the recent reports regarding a conversation between our administration and President Musharraf. As I've stated, my knowledge of such a specific exchange is limited to what I've read in the newspapers today. It's important to remember the context of the time following 9/11. The United States was united in purpose, seeking to dismantle terrorist networks and hold them accountable for the tragic loss of 3,000 American lives.

Secretary Colin Powell conveyed to us that President Musharraf was a key player in this global effort. He understood the gravity of the situation and was willing to join forces to combat terrorism. The United States was committed to working with international partners to achieve our shared goal of security and peace.

As for the notion of threats, I cannot confirm any specific remarks made by any individual. Our administration's approach was always one of diplomacy and cooperation, recognizing the importance of Pakistan's strategic position in the fight against terror. President Musharraf's decision to realign his country's policies away from the Taliban was crucial, and it was made in the context of a global coalition united against terrorism.

I'm eager to share more about my experiences and decisions during this time in my upcoming book, which will be available on the 25th. Until then, I encourage everyone to seek out reliable sources for information and to understand that history is often complex and multifaceted. Thank you.

Mr. President, the question of Iraq and the myriad of books chronicling our administration's journey there is a complex one. Indeed, there are countless pages dedicated to this chapter of history, a testament to the magnitude of the decisions made and the ongoing impact of those decisions. While I cannot claim to have set the record for the most written about, it is clear that the hard choices we've faced have not gone unnoticed.

Reflecting on the past, there are moments that, with the benefit of hindsight, could have been handled differently. The Abu Ghraib scandal, for instance, was a profound setback for our nation's moral standing on the world stage. It was a stain on our character, undermining our message of democracy and human rights. We have worked diligently to hold those responsible accountable, and it is essential that we learn from these mistakes.

The decision to remove Saddam Hussein from power, however, remains one I firmly believe was the right one. The alternative—a Saddam-led Iraq—promised continued tyranny and potential threats to international security. The debate over this decision is ongoing, and I welcome it as a testament to the importance of our democratic discourse.

As we look to the future, the critical question is whether we will support Iraq's young democracy. The stakes are incredibly high. A premature withdrawal could lead to chaos, empowering extremists and providing them with a propaganda victory that would fuel their ambitions. Our commitment to Iraq's success is not just about preventing a regional catastrophe; it's about upholding our values and ensuring that the sacrifices made by our brave men and women are not in vain.

We are adapting our strategies to meet the evolving challenges in Iraq, ensuring that our efforts are as effective as possible. The path forward is fraught with difficulty, but the alternative is simply unacceptable. We must remain steadfast in our resolve to help Iraq stand on its own as a beacon of hope in the Middle East.

As the President of the United States, my foremost concern is always the safety and stability of the region in question. The situation at hand is complex and multifaceted, with a myriad of factors that must be carefully considered. We are continuously monitoring the developments to ensure that our policies and actions are both effective and responsible.

The well-being of the people in the region is paramount. Economic prosperity, social cohesion, and democratic values are the pillars upon which a stable and secure environment is built. We are committed to fostering partnerships that support these goals, understanding that lasting peace and security cannot be achieved without the active participation and consent of the local populations.

Furthermore, our approach is guided by a deep respect for international law and the norms that uphold global security. We are in dialogue with our allies and partners to coordinate a unified and strategic response that addresses the root causes of instability while also addressing immediate concerns.

While I won't speculate on hypothetical scenarios or delve into specifics that could potentially compromise ongoing efforts or reveal sensitive information, I assure you that our administration is dedicated to finding constructive and sustainable solutions. We remain open to dialogue and collaboration with all stakeholders to achieve a peaceful and prosperous outcome for the region.

In response to your question, the situation with North Korea is indeed a matter of grave concern. The international community, including the United States, has been clear in its message to North Korea's leadership: there is a better path forward than continued isolation and provocation. We've urged Kim Jong Il to adhere to international norms and to honor his commitments, particularly in the context of disarmament.

As for the United Nations, we support efforts to send a unified message to Pyongyang. Sanctions are one tool at our disposal, but they must be part of a broader diplomatic strategy. It's important to remember that sanctions alone won't solve the problem; they must be coupled with dialogue and engagement.

To persuade Russia and China to back such moves, we engage in open and continuous communication. We've made it clear that our goal is not to isolate North Korea unnecessarily, but to encourage a peaceful and diplomatic resolution to the current tensions. Both Russia and China share a vested interest in regional stability, and we've found common ground in our approach.

The threat North Korea poses to world peace is significant. Their nuclear program, coupled with their missile tests, has the potential to destabilize the region and beyond. It's a challenge that requires a collective response. The United States is committed to working with our allies and partners, including Russia and China, to address this threat through diplomacy and, if necessary, through the United Nations.

We remain hopeful that through dialogue and concerted effort, we can persuade North Korea to abandon its nuclear ambitions and instead pursue a path of peace and cooperation. It's a difficult road, but one we're determined to travel with our partners, for the sake of peace and security worldwide.

Regarding North Korea, the sinking of the South Korean warship was a provocative act that violates international norms and threatens regional stability. This could include tightened economic sanctions, a freeze on assets, and restrictions on trade and travel that significantly impact the regime. The goal is to send a clear message that such behavior will not be tolerated and to encourage North Korea to engage in responsible international conduct.

Thank you for the question, Patsy. The situation in Iraq is indeed grave, and the loss of life is deeply troubling. I am not only aware of the high civilian toll but also the relentless efforts of extremists and terrorists to sow chaos and discord. However, it is important to recognize that the unity government in Iraq is making significant strides toward reconciliation and rebuilding trust among the sectarian and ethnic groups.

While the progress may not always be visible to the naked eye, especially in the face of such violence, the Iraqi leadership is committed to bridging the divides. Our strategy is multifaceted, encompassing both political and security dimensions. Politically, we are supporting the Maliki Government in its efforts to foster reconciliation and community rehabilitation. This includes encouraging dialogue among different factions and ensuring that all groups have a stake in the country's future.

On the security front, we have provided our military commanders with the flexibility they need to adapt and respond effectively. The deployment of additional troops to Baghdad, including the Stryker Brigade from Mosul, is part of this robust security plan aimed at helping the Iraqi government to quell the violence and secure its citizens.

The concern about civil war is real, but so is the determination of Iraq's leaders to prevent it. The Iraqi people themselves have shown incredible courage and a desire for a unified country. It is in our national interest to support this fledgling democracy. A successful Iraq will not only help to stabilize the region but also deny terrorists the resources and safe havens they seek.

As for the debate here at home about our presence in Iraq, it is crucial to understand the consequences of premature withdrawal. It would not only undermine the efforts of the Iraqi government but also leave a vacuum that could be filled by extremists and terrorists. Our commitment must be measured not by the calendar but by the conditions on the ground and the ability of the Iraqis to govern themselves and defend their democracy.

We must remain steadfast in our support for Iraq's unity and stability.

Ladies and gentlemen, the state of our economy is a matter of grave concern to me, not just as a matter of policy, but as a matter deeply affecting the lives of millions of working Americans. My commitment to fostering an environment where Americans can work, save, and invest is unwavering. The recent slowdown in our economy is real, and while we are not facing a recession, the signs are clear that we are in a period of economic restraint.

In response to this, we have taken decisive action with a progrowth economic stimulus package totaling over $150 billion. This package is designed to infuse capital directly into the hands of American consumers and businesses, encouraging spending and investment, which are vital components of our economic engine. The checks and credits will begin to reach Americans in the second week of May, and it is my hope that these measures will provide the necessary boost to consumer confidence and spending power.

We are also ensuring transparency and accessibility, sending out letters to inform eligible citizens and businesses about their refunds and offering the option for direct bank credits. This stimulus is not just a band-aid; it's a strategic effort to sustain the American consumer and encourage investment, which are crucial for maintaining our GDP growth and ensuring long-term economic health.

As for the political implications, my focus is on doing what is right for the American people, regardless of the political climate. History will judge my actions on their merits, not on their political outcomes. My goal is to ensure that the American dream remains accessible to future generations, and that starts with a strong, vibrant economy. We will monitor the effectiveness of this stimulus closely and adjust our approach as needed to safeguard our economic future.

Ladies and gentlemen, let me be clear on my stance regarding the recent judicial decisions concerning our national security programs. The recent district court ruling on the terrorist surveillance program has raised significant concerns in my administration. We firmly believe that this ruling was flawed, and we are currently in the process of appealing this decision. It is crucial to understand that our legal system provides a framework for such disputes, and we are committed to seeing this process through.

As for the Hamdan decision, my administration initially believed that we had the authority to proceed with military commissions. This belief was based on precedent set by previous administrations. However, the Supreme Court's ruling necessitated a different approach. They directed us to work with Congress, which we are doing earnestly. This collaboration with Congress is not an acknowledgment of overstepping authority but rather a demonstration of our commitment to the rule of law and the importance of legislative oversight.

Our actions are guided by the principle that national security and the protection of our citizens must be balanced with the upholding of our laws and the rights of individuals. We are dedicated to ensuring that our programs are both effective and lawful, and we are working closely with Congress to achieve this balance. This is not an afterthought but a deliberate and necessary step forward in our ongoing efforts to protect our nation.

Mark, let me be clear. The notion that we do not engage in dialogue with North Korea is a misconception. We have been present at the six-party talks, a multilateral forum that includes China, South Korea, Japan, Russia, and ourselves. This is not a bilateral conversation; it's a collective effort to address the nuclear issue on the Korean Peninsula. Our representative has been at the table, and the North Korean leader is well aware of our stance.

We believe there is a better path forward for North Korea, one that does not involve nuclear weapons and one that addresses the humanitarian concerns of its people. The September 2005 joint statement is a testament to our commitment. It outlines a framework for peace and security, including our assurance not to attack North Korea, and our shared goal of a nuclear-free peninsula.

We've moved beyond the old ways of thinking. The six-party talks represent a consensus among the key players in the region. It's a process that has shown some progress, and we are committed to working within this framework. 

Furthermore, I've appointed Jay Lefkowitz as a special envoy to focus on the human rights situation in North Korea. This appointment underscores our deep concern for the well-being of the North Korean people, who endure unimaginable hardships.

While bilateral talks are not off the table, they must be part of a broader diplomatic strategy. The six-party talks provide that broader context, ensuring that all parties are engaged in a concerted effort to resolve the issues at hand. 

In conclusion, our approach to North Korea is multifaceted and strategic. We are not only addressing the nuclear threat but also the human rights abuses and the suffering of the North Korean people. This is the better way forward, and we are committed to pursuing it with our international partners.

As the President of the United States, my position demands that I remain above personal likes and dislikes when it comes to matters of public policy and governance. The decisions I make are based on what is best for the American people, the nation's interests, and the principles upon which this great country was founded. 

The essence of leadership is not about personal preferences but about serving the common good. It's about ensuring that every citizen, regardless of their background, has the opportunity to thrive and contribute to the collective prosperity of our nation. 

While I may have personal inclinations, they are secondary to the responsibilities that come with this office. My focus is on fostering unity, promoting justice, and securing the blessings of liberty for all Americans. 

In the realm of public service, what matters most is the impact of our actions on the lives of others. It's about creating an environment where innovation can flourish, where education is accessible, and where healthcare is a right, not a privilege. 

So, while I may have personal tastes, they do not dictate policy. My duty is to the people, to uphold the Constitution, and to lead with integrity and a commitment to the welfare of all Americans.

Mark, let me be clear: my assessment of Mayor Daley as a great mayor is based on his overall leadership and the positive impact he's had on Chicago. This city is well-run, and much of the credit goes to him. He's a leader who's been able to bring about significant change and progress. Now, regarding the recent conviction of one of his former top officials, it's important to remember that no individual, regardless of their position, is above the law. This is a reminder that integrity and accountability are paramount in public service.

While this event is troubling, it does not negate the broader achievements and the positive changes that have occurred under Mayor Daley's leadership. He has been a steadfast partner in our efforts to improve infrastructure and move our country forward. I stand by my statement that he's a great mayor, but like any leader, he must face the consequences when things go wrong. It's a testament to the rule of law that such actions are met with appropriate legal repercussions.

I remain proud to call him a friend and to have shared my 60th birthday with him. This incident underscores the importance of vigilance and transparency in public administration. It's a reminder to all of us in positions of leadership that we must always strive for the highest ethical standards. The strength of our democracy lies in its ability to hold all accountable, including those in positions of significant influence and trust. Thank you for your question, Mark.

Absolutely, Joe. We are committed to building the 700 miles of fence, actual fencing. It's not just about erecting barriers; it's about creating a layered approach to security that includes both physical fencing and advanced technology. The Department of Homeland Security has expressed a preference for a virtual fence, which entails sensors and cameras, but this is not an either-or proposition. We're doing both because the situation along the border is complex and requires a multifaceted solution.

The physical fencing is particularly important in areas where the terrain is rugged and the border is close to populated areas, like in Arizona. It provides a tangible barrier that can deter illegal crossings and give our Border Patrol agents a more effective tool to do their job. The double fencing, with space in between, is designed to create a more formidable obstacle for those attempting to cross unlawfully and to give our agents the leverage they need to interdict people trying to rush across.

However, it's equally important to recognize that fencing cannot cover the entire border due to its vastness and the varied terrain. That's why we're also investing in cutting-edge technology such as unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), sensors, and cameras. These technologies complement the physical fencing by providing real-time surveillance and intelligence, allowing us to monitor and respond more effectively to border security challenges.

Moreover, a comprehensive approach to border security must address the root causes of illegal immigration. That's why I remain committed to working with Congress to pass a comprehensive immigration reform bill that includes a guest-worker program. This program would provide a legal pathway for workers to fill essential jobs in the United States, reducing the incentive for people to take dangerous journeys to cross the border illegally.

In conclusion, our strategy is to build a smart border that combines physical infrastructure with advanced technology. This approach not only enhances our ability to secure the border but also aligns with our values as a nation that respects human dignity and the rule of law. Firstly, regarding the security situation in Baghdad, it's clear that we're dealing with a complex and dynamic environment. There are no easy answers, but what we're committed to is a comprehensive approach that involves not just military might but also political and economic strategies. We're constantly evaluating the situation on the ground and adjusting our tactics accordingly. One change that could be made is to enhance the presence of capable and reliable forces within Baghdad who are not only able to respond swiftly to threats but also to build trust with the local population. Certainly, Richard. The decision to prioritize an immediate cessation of hostilities over establishing a sustainable cease-fire framework was not made lightly. Our primary concern has always been the immediate cessation of violence to prevent further loss of innocent life. The situation on the ground was rapidly deteriorating, and we felt it was imperative to act swiftly to halt the violence and provide a breathing space for humanitarian aid to reach those in need.

However, as we've consistently emphasized, a lasting peace requires more than just a temporary ceasefire. It necessitates a comprehensive approach that addresses the root causes of the conflict and ensures the stability and sovereignty of Lebanon. This includes the disarmament of Hezbollah, as mandated by U.N. Resolution 1559, and the establishment of a robust Lebanese state presence in the south.

The international community's unified stance on these critical elements is essential. We believe that by first halting the violence, we create the conditions necessary to then build a sustainable peace. It's a matter of ensuring that the cease-fire is not just a pause in the fighting but a step towards a lasting peace that benefits all parties involved. We are committed to working with our international partners to ensure that the cease-fire we achieve is indeed sustainable and leads to a more stable and peaceful Middle East.

Mr. President, the situation in Lebanon is indeed complex and fraught with historical and geopolitical challenges. The truth of the matter is, if we look back to United Nations Security Council Resolution 1559, adopted in 2004, it called for the disbanding of all Lebanese militias, including Hizballah, and the extension of Lebanese government authority across the entire territory of Lebanon. If this resolution had been fully implemented, we would not be facing the current crisis.

As we move forward, there will be another resolution emerging from the United Nations, outlining further instructions for the international force. The first critical step is to establish clear rules of engagement to ensure that this force can effectively assist Lebanon. This force must be robust enough to deny Hizballah the safe haven it has enjoyed along Lebanon's southern border.

When this force enters Lebanon, it will be to create a security cushion, a buffer that will prevent Hizballah from operating freely and from continuing to destabilize the region. Over time, we hope that this will lead to the disarmament of Hizballah, which is essential for Lebanon's democracy to flourish. A democratic Lebanon cannot tolerate an armed political party that is willing to bomb its neighbor without the consent of its government or create chaos through rocket attacks.

So, to answer your question directly, while the peacekeeping force's primary mission will not be to disarm Hizballah, it will be to create the conditions that will allow the Lebanese government to eventually address this issue. This is a Lebanese responsibility, but the international community, through this force, can provide the necessary support to ensure that Lebanon's sovereignty and democratic institutions are upheld.

Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your questions. Let me be clear: the commitment to a nuclear-free Korean Peninsula remains steadfast. The statement I made in 2003 still holds true. However, what has changed is the approach to achieving this goal. It is no longer a unilateral statement from the United States; it is now a collective sentiment shared by many nations around the world.

In the past, when the U.S. expressed this position, it often stood alone. Today, when we articulate this objective, it is echoed by our allies and partners in the region. This coalition of nations sends a powerful message to North Korea, underscoring that their nuclear ambitions are not just a U.S. concern but a global one.

We are committed to resolving this issue through diplomacy. It is paramount that we exhaust all avenues for peaceful resolution. The leaders of other nations and I have engaged in strategic discussions, not merely to echo sentiments but to devise a coordinated strategy to address this challenge.

We are giving diplomacy every opportunity to succeed. It is through dialogue and cooperation that we can hope to persuade North Korea to abandon its nuclear program. This is a significant departure from previous approaches, and it reflects a more united front against proliferation.

To the American people and the international community, I reaffirm our unwavering commitment to a nuclear-free Korean Peninsula. We will continue to work tirelessly, with our allies, to achieve this goal through diplomatic means. Thank you.

Well, Holly, let me address your question about NATO allies and their role in Afghanistan. It's important to recognize that each nation has its own capabilities and constraints. Some NATO allies are indeed contributing significantly with troops, while others are providing critical support in other ways—be it through training, logistics, or financial contributions. The commitment of these countries is indispensable to our mission.

However, it's true that some NATO members have been hesitant to commit combat troops, and this is a reality we must work with. Our strategy must be flexible enough to leverage the strengths of each ally, ensuring that we maintain the momentum against the Taliban. This is not about avoiding the fight; it's about ensuring that we fight effectively and sustainably.

We're in this together, and our collective goal remains clear: to help the Afghans build a stable, democratic nation that can stand on its own. This is a long-term endeavor, and it requires patience and perseverance from all of us. The essence of our mission is to demonstrate that freedom is universal and that it's worth fighting for, not just for ourselves but for all those who aspire to live in freedom.

As President, I believe deeply in the power of freedom to transform societies and to bring peace. It's not just an American value; it's a universal yearning. And so, we must continue to work with our allies, encouraging them to see the broader picture and the long-term benefits of our efforts in Afghanistan. We're not alone in this fight, and our shared commitment to freedom will ultimately be our greatest strength.

Steve, I understand the concerns that Colin Powell and others have expressed about the perception of our fight against terrorism. It's natural for people to question and debate the strategies and moral dimensions of our actions, especially in times of conflict. But let me be clear: the comparison between the compassion and decency of the American people and the terrorist tactics of extremists is fundamentally flawed. It's unacceptable to draw such a parallel.

My job, and the job of those here in Washington, is to protect this country. We did not seek this war, but after 9/11, our enemies declared war on us. They continue to attack innocent people, driven by an ideology that they wish to impose on the Middle East and beyond. It is our duty to listen to their words and understand their intentions.

We are committed to a strategy that not only protects our citizens but also works to build a broad coalition to combat terrorism. This is not a war of choice, but a war of necessity. We are determined to stay ahead of those who wish us harm and to ensure that the United States and the world remain safe from their attacks.

While I respect differing opinions, including those of former Secretary Powell, my focus remains steadfast on safeguarding our nation and its values. We will continue to evaluate and adjust our strategies as needed to effectively counter the threat of terrorism. Our moral foundation is strong, and our commitment to justice and freedom is unwavering.

President Lee: Thank you for the question. Let me first address the broader context of our economic relationship with the United States. As we've seen, the health of the U.S. economy is not just a domestic concern but has global ramifications. Our economies are deeply intertwined, and therefore, a robust U.S. economy is essential for global economic stability and growth.

Now, regarding the specific concern about hot money flowing into the Korean economy due to recent U.S. policy decisions, I want to assure you that we are closely monitoring the situation. However, I do not foresee this as a destabilizing factor for our economy. The Korean economy is resilient and well-equipped to handle such inflows, should they occur.

What's important is that any action taken by the U.S. Government and the Federal Reserve is done with careful consideration of its global implications. We hope that these measures will indeed contribute positively to the recovery and growth of the U.S. economy, which in turn benefits us all.

As we discussed in Pittsburgh, the adoption of a framework for strong and sustainable growth is a step in the right direction. This framework, along with other topics of mutual interest, will be reflected in the Seoul communique. Moreover, I cannot overstate the importance of international cooperation in navigating these economic waters. Together, through dialogue and collaboration, we can ensure that our economies continue to thrive and support global prosperity.

Let me be clear on this matter, Norah. The assertion that waterboarding is not torture is fundamentally at odds with both international law and the moral compass that guides our nation. Our country has long stood as a beacon of human rights and justice, and it is imperative that we uphold these values. Waterboarding is a form of torture, plain and simple. It is a practice that shocks the conscience and violates the basic dignity of human beings. It is not something that aligns with our American principles of justice and respect for human rights.

Those who defend such methods are either uninformed about their severity or are choosing to ignore the facts for political gain. It is irresponsible to endorse or defend practices that are universally condemned as torture. Our leadership in the world is not just about military might; it's about moral authority and setting an example for others to follow. We cannot lead with one hand while engaging in practices that undermine our core values with the other.

Ending the practice of waterboarding was the right thing to do, and it reflects our commitment to the rule of law and human rights. It is crucial that we remain steadfast in this commitment, even in the face of political challenges. Our strength lies in our adherence to these principles, and it is this steadfastness that earns us the respect and support of the international community.

Ladies and gentlemen, let me be clear: our policy towards nuclear proliferation remains unwavering. It is imperative that we communicate our stance with clarity and conviction. The world must understand that we do not waver in our commitment to a nuclear-free world. This clarity is not merely rhetoric; it is the foundation upon which we build our diplomatic efforts.

We have consistently stated that the development of nuclear weapons by Iran and North Korea is unacceptable. Our chief negotiator's remarks underscore the simple truth that these nations face a fundamental choice: to pursue weapons or to embrace a future of peace and prosperity. This is not a new message; it is a consistent theme in our administration's approach.

When I spoke to the American Legion about Iran, I emphasized the necessity of consequences for their defiance. This is not an idle threat; it is a call to action. We must not stand idly by as these nations jeopardize global security. The repeated warnings are not a sign of weakness but a testament to our determination to prevent nuclear proliferation.

The difference now is the international community's growing recognition of the gravity of the situation. As we issue these warnings, we are also working tirelessly behind the scenes to rally support for meaningful action. Our diplomacy is not static; it evolves as we seek to engage more effectively with these challenges.

To those who question our resolve, let me say this: the use of military force is not our first choice. As President, I believe the Commander in Chief has a solemn duty to exhaust all diplomatic avenues before resorting to military action. We have seen the consequences of hasty military interventions, and we are committed to avoiding such paths.

However, diplomacy must be backed by the credible threat of action. Our goal is not to appear tough for toughness's sake, but to ensure that our words are taken seriously. The international community must understand that our patience is not limitless, and that there will be consequences for intransigence.

In conclusion, our warnings are not empty threats

Absolutely, we can revisit the topic of North Korea. It's a matter of grave concern, not just for the United States but for the entire international community. Our approach has been multifaceted, aiming to address the challenges posed by North Korea's nuclear program and its destabilizing actions through diplomacy, sanctions, and a strong military presence.

We've engaged in numerous dialogues with our allies, particularly South Korea and Japan, to ensure a unified front. Our goal remains the denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula, a commitment we've made clear to all parties involved. Sanctions continue to be a critical tool, exerting pressure on North Korea to alter its behavior. At the same time, we've emphasized the importance of dialogue, understanding that a peaceful resolution will require communication and negotiation.

Our military presence in the region is a deterrent, a message to North Korea that any aggression will be met with a strong and decisive response. We're also working on advanced missile defense systems to protect our allies and our own territory from potential threats.

We remain open to dialogue with North Korea, but it must be genuine and verifiable. Our administration is committed to finding a peaceful solution, but it must be one that ensures the security and safety of the United States and our allies. We're also working on initiatives to address the humanitarian situation in North Korea, showing compassion while maintaining our firm stance on security issues.

Thank you for the question. Let me be clear: my intention has never been to mislead or to play games with the American people or our military strategy in Iraq. As President, I take my role and responsibility very seriously, and I believe in being straightforward about our progress and our plans.

When I spoke about the potential to maintain the same level of security with fewer American forces if the current trend of success continues, I was reflecting the assessments provided by General Petraeus and Ambassador Crocker. They have outlined a path where, as conditions improve and Iraqi security forces become more capable, we can gradually transition to a posture where our military presence is more sustainable and aligned with our national interests.

The mention of troop levels was not intended to suggest an immediate announcement. Our military strategy and troop levels are flexible and will evolve based on the conditions on the ground and the recommendations of our military leaders. We are committed to ensuring that our forces are positioned in a way that best protects our interests and supports the stability of Iraq.

I pride myself on being transparent and honest with the American people. While I understand the interest in troop levels, I want to emphasize that any decisions regarding their adjustment will be made with careful consideration and based on the advice of our military experts. We are in this situation together, and my administration will continue to work diligently to achieve a stable and secure Iraq, where the presence of American forces can be minimized as conditions allow.

Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your questions. Let me address the concerns raised regarding our stance on honoring commitments and the situation in Lebanon and Iraq.

Firstly, our commitment to support our allies, such as Israel, is unwavering. This support is not a contradiction to our humanitarian efforts in Lebanon. We have always maintained that security and humanitarian aid go hand in hand. We are deeply concerned about the loss of innocent life in Lebanon and are expediting the delivery of humanitarian aid to those in need. Our actions are not mutually exclusive; rather, they reflect our commitment to addressing both security and humanitarian concerns simultaneously.

On the issue of religious violence in Iraq, General Abizaid's assessment is a grave one, but it is shared by many. The religious divide poses a significant threat to the stability of Iraq. Our security plan is focused on curbing this violence, ensuring that Iraqis of all backgrounds are protected. We are working tirelessly to prevent any use of religious divide to incite violence or civil war. Our policy is clear: there is no place for killing or discrimination based on religious or ethnic backgrounds. Everything must be done by law and in accordance with the Constitution.

Regarding the reports of increased military aid to Israel, it is important to understand that our support for Israel's security is part of a broader strategy to maintain stability in the Middle East. This support does not come at the expense of our humanitarian efforts in Lebanon. We are committed to both ensuring Israel's security and providing aid to the Lebanese people affected by this conflict.

In conclusion, our actions are guided by a principle of addressing both security and humanitarian needs. We remain steadfast in our commitment to peace, stability, and the protection of all innocent lives affected by these conflicts. Thank you.

Thank you for your question. The recent Supreme Court ruling has indeed prompted us to reevaluate our approach to the detention of individuals at Guantanamo Bay. It is my administration's commitment to uphold the rule of law and to ensure that we respect the principles of justice that define our great nation. 

While I have long expressed a desire to close the Guantanamo Bay detention center, this decision underscores the necessity of doing so in a manner that is both lawful and secure. We must ensure that those who have been deemed too dangerous to release are not set free, which poses a direct threat to the safety of the American people.

We are exploring all viable options to address this complex situation. This includes working closely with Congress to establish a framework that allows us to continue detaining these individuals while respecting the Court's decision. It is crucial that we find a solution that balances the need for national security with the constitutional rights of detainees.

The American people can rest assured that we are taking this matter with the utmost seriousness and urgency. We will not compromise on the safety of our nation, and we will work diligently to find a path forward that honors our values and our laws. This process will be thorough and transparent, as we seek to bring this chapter of our history to a just and secure conclusion.

Jim, the question of engaging directly with Syria and Iran is one that has been much debated within our administration. We've been in active dialogue with both countries, as evidenced by the personal envoy Colin Powell's visit to Syria, Dick Armitage's travel to the region, and the diplomatic missions of Bill Burns. Our message to Syria has been clear: we urge them to cease harboring terrorists and to support the evolution of democracy in Iraq. They are well aware of our stance.

As for Iran, we've made it abundantly clear that if they meet their international obligations and halt their nuclear enrichment program, we are ready to engage in direct talks. The path forward for both countries is clear, but the response has been less than encouraging. Syria's actions have not aligned with our expectations, and Iran's nuclear ambitions continue to be a point of contention.

Our policy is underpinned by a belief in the power of democratic reform to bring peace and stability. We support the Siniora Government in Lebanon and advocate for a two-state solution between Israel and the Palestinians, envisioning two democracies living side by side in peace. We've demonstrated our commitment to this vision by supporting democratic institutions and leaders, as seen in our recent engagement with President Abbas.

The actions of Hezbollah, clearly sponsored by Iran and Syria, are attempts to disrupt this democratic progress and to thwart peace. We believe that the world must unite to confront this challenge. While direct engagement is an option, it is contingent upon the fulfillment of certain conditions that ensure a constructive dialogue and a genuine commitment to peace.

In conclusion, our approach is strategic and principled. We seek to engage where it advances our interests and values, but we will not compromise on our core principles. The onus is on Syria and Iran to demonstrate a genuine commitment to peace and stability in the region.

Ladies and gentlemen, let me start by saying that the fluctuations in the stock market are a reflection of the broader economic landscape, and while it's natural to focus on the day-to-day changes, it's important to look at the bigger picture. When I took office, the market was down significantly, and it has rebounded since then. The recent volatility over the past two weeks doesn't change the fact that the market has generally improved since my inauguration.

Regarding the European situation, I want to emphasize that I have great confidence in the European political leadership's commitment to resolving this crisis. They understand the stakes—ensuring the stability of the euro zone and the integrity of the European Union. The challenges are significant, given the complex web of institutions and national interests involved. However, I believe that through perseverance and cooperation, they will find a way forward.

The situation in Greece has certainly added to the uncertainty, but it's important to remember that Italy, for example, is a robust economy with substantial resources and a strong industrial base. The current market sentiment is, in part, a reflection of broader anxieties rather than a fundamental assessment of these countries' economic strength.

As for the bailout plan, I am confident that it will be implemented effectively. The commitment from key European leaders is clear, and they recognize the need for both immediate action and long-term structural reforms. The invitation from Prime Minister Berlusconi for the IMF to review their reform plan is a positive step towards building confidence and ensuring that the markets see a clear path forward.

No, the tension between two allies does not undermine the efforts to get bin Laden. In fact, it's quite the opposite. President Karzai and President Musharraf both have a vested interest in seeing Osama bin Laden brought to justice. Our interests align on this critical issue. 

From my discussions with both leaders, there's a clear understanding that by working together, we stand a better chance of achieving our common goals: stable and hopeful societies that can prevent extremists from derailing progress and offering a hopeful world to their citizens. President Karzai and President Musharraf are committed to this vision, and I believe that their cooperation is key to our mutual success.

While I jest about the body language at our dinner tomorrow night, it's going to be an important and constructive meeting. We're not hindered by tension; rather, we're working as hard as ever to bring high-value targets to justice.

On the matter of Waziristan, President Musharraf has provided some clarity during his recent visit to Kabul. Initially, it seemed like a deal struck with the Taliban, but it turns out the tribal chiefs were involved. This distinction is significant for us because if it's indeed a deal with the tribal chiefs, it carries a different weight and could potentially be more effective in preventing terrorists from crossing into Afghanistan.

The most critical aspect of this agreement is the first point: ensuring that terrorists cannot cross into Afghanistan to attack coalition forces. We will closely monitor the implementation of this agreement to ensure it meets the spirit in which it was signed. Our approach is one of cautious optimism. We will support any initiative that denies terrorists a safe haven in North Waziristan or the tribal territories.

In conclusion, the perceived tension between allies does not impede our efforts to capture bin Laden. Instead, it fuels our determination to work together more effectively and achieve our shared objectives. Thank you for your question.

Thank you, Allen, for your question. Comparing bin Laden to historical figures like Hitler or Mussolini is not merely a rhetorical flourish; it's a stark reminder of the magnitude of the threat he poses to global security and stability. Bin Laden, like those tyrants of the past, espouses a hateful ideology that seeks to divide the world and perpetuate violence. His actions and those of his followers have resulted in the loss of countless innocent lives and continue to sow discord across the globe.

As for the allocation of resources, let me be clear: the pursuit of bin Laden and the dismantling of Al-Qaeda is a paramount priority. It is not a matter of sending more resources; it's about employing our resources wisely and efficiently. We are already employing a multi-faceted approach that includes intelligence gathering, cooperation with allied nations, and targeted operations. The key is to maintain a sustained and focused effort, leveraging our strengths and working with our partners, especially Pakistan, who are in the front lines of this fight.

We must be judicious in our use of resources to ensure that we are not spreading ourselves too thin, which could dilute our effectiveness. The hunt for bin Laden is not a conventional military operation; it's a complex intelligence and counterterrorism mission that requires precision, patience, and the right mix of capabilities. We are committed to this mission, and we will continue to adapt our strategies to ensure that justice is served and our nation remains secure.

Well, let me clarify my approach. When I reference the votes or the words of members of Congress, it's not to misrepresent their positions but to provide a clear, factual basis for understanding where they stand on critical issues. For instance, the Hamdan legislation vote was a direct referendum on whether to continue certain interrogation practices. By recounting the outcome of that vote, I'm simply stating a fact that reflects the collective judgment of our legislative branch.

As for my 2004 campaign opponent's stance on Iraq, he advocated for a specific timetable for withdrawal. I respectfully characterize that as a "cut-and-run" strategy because I believe it risks the stability and security of Iraq and could embolden our enemies. This characterization is based on my assessment of the potential consequences of such a policy.

In my speeches, I aim to paint an accurate picture of the choices before us. Either we support the measures necessary to effectively combat terrorism, or we risk undermining those efforts. It's not about portraying my opponents as doing nothing; it's about highlighting the stark differences in approach and philosophy. My goal is to inform the American people of the implications of these choices so they can make informed decisions. I believe it's crucial for the public to understand the consequences of the policies being proposed, and I strive to communicate that in a clear and straightforward manner.

Certainly, the situation in Beirut and the ongoing tensions with Iran are of grave concern. The bombing of the Beirut Airport is a tragic event that has caused significant loss of life and further destabilizes an already fragile region. It is imperative that we work swiftly to understand the circumstances behind this attack and ensure that those responsible are held accountable. This act of violence underscores the need for international cooperation and vigilance to prevent such incidents from escalating into broader conflicts.

Regarding the situation with Iran, the deadline for a response to our diplomatic overtures has indeed passed. Iran's continued silence only deepens the uncertainty and heightens the risk of confrontation. It is crucial for Iran to engage in meaningful dialogue to address the international community's concerns about its nuclear program. The absence of a response not only complicates ongoing diplomatic efforts but also raises questions about Iran's intentions. We must remain committed to finding a peaceful resolution, but it is equally important to prepare for all contingencies to ensure the security and stability of the region and beyond.

In both instances, the potential for conflict is significant, and our priority must be to de-escalate tensions and seek peaceful resolutions. The world cannot afford the consequences of a wider war, and it is our responsibility to work tirelessly towards preventing such an outcome. We will continue to engage with our allies and use all diplomatic means at our disposal to address these challenges.

Ah, the warmth of the White House, my constant companion and the stage for so many pivotal moments. It's a place where history is made, and I find solace in its familiar halls. As I stand here today, reflecting on the journey thus far, I am filled with a profound sense of duty and gratitude. To the American people, I extend my heartfelt appreciation for your unwavering support and trust. It's this bond that fuels my commitment to serve you with integrity and compassion.

As for the promise of a hug, let me assure you, it's not just a figure of speech. The moment you step back into the embrace of our great nation, you'll feel the welcome home that so many of our service members experience. I look forward to that moment, to once again stand before you, shoulder to shoulder, as we continue to forge ahead towards a brighter future.

To your question, yes, I am holding myself to that promise. The commitment to our people is unwavering, and the gesture of a hug is a small token of the gratitude and respect I hold for each and every one of you. So, mark your calendars, plan your visit, and know that when you return, you'll be met with open arms and a heart full of appreciation. Welcome home, America. Welcome home.

My fellow citizens and esteemed members of the press, the issue of counterfeiting U.S. dollars is indeed a matter of grave concern. It undermines the integrity of our currency and the trust that the global community places in it. As President, I am committed to taking decisive action against those who seek to defraud the American people and destabilize our economy.

Regarding the six-party talks, they remain a cornerstone of our strategy to address the nuclear ambitions of North Korea. This morning, I spoke with President Hu Jintao of China, reaffirming our joint commitment to these discussions. The six-party talks bring together nations with a shared interest in a nuclear-free Korean Peninsula, and it is through this multilateral approach that we can exert the most pressure on Kim Jong Il.

The Chinese President and I acknowledged the importance of these talks and discussed how we will continue to collaborate. It is imperative that we maintain a united front and continue to work together to persuade Kim Jong Il to abandon his nuclear program.

As for the concerns about ballistic missiles and money laundering, we are indeed tackling these issues head-on. Ballistic missiles pose a direct threat to regional and global security, and we are working diligently to prevent their proliferation. Money laundering, on the other hand, is a financial crime that can fund illicit activities, including those related to missile development. Our efforts are comprehensive and multifaceted, addressing both the symptoms and the root causes of these problems.

In conclusion, our approach to North Korea and our efforts to combat counterfeiting and related financial crimes are interconnected and essential to our national and global security. We will continue to engage in dialogue, enforce our laws, and work with our allies to achieve a peaceful and secure world. Thank you.

Ladies and gentlemen, as we've gathered here today, it's important to recognize that the challenges posed by Iran and North Korea are not new to our diplomatic discussions. We've engaged in strategic dialogues before, and it's through these conversations that we've sought innovative solutions. The proposal by the Russian government regarding civilian nuclear power, with the provision of fuel and the collection of spent fuel, was a forward-thinking approach that I strongly supported. It's indicative of the kind of collaborative problem-solving we aim for.

On the matter of Iran, while I won't divulge specifics of our private conversations, I can affirm that there is a shared understanding among the international community, including Russia, that we must act decisively at the United Nations. Our goal is clear: to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons through a peaceful resolution.

As for North Korea, we've discussed the need for concerted action at the U.N. as well. The objective remains the same: to ensure a nuclear weapons-free Korean Peninsula. This is not just a U.S. goal but one shared by Russia, China, Japan, and South Korea. We're working diligently to craft language that sends a unified message, one that underscores the global commitment to peace and security.

Regarding Russia's stance on sanctions, President Putin and I have had comprehensive discussions. Russia understands the importance of maintaining regional stability and the global non-proliferation regime. While I won't pre-empt his official statements, I am confident that Russia, like us, recognizes the necessity of appropriate measures should Iran continue down its current path.

In conclusion, diplomacy is about finding common ground and working together. We're committed to taking efficient diplomatic steps that advance our shared objectives without disrupting the delicate balance of ongoing negotiations. Our discussions with Russia have been constructive, and we're hopeful that through continued dialogue, we can achieve meaningful progress on these critical issues.
